articles.title: Targeting long non-coding RNAs to improve therapeutic response in nervous system tumours.
articles.abstract: Despite advances in surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and targeted treatments, resistance remains a major obstacle in nervous system (NS) tumours. Treatment failure reflects not only individual oncogenic alterations but also adaptive regulatory networks that enable tumour cells to survive therapeutic stress, maintain plasticity and adopt therapy-tolerant phenotypes. Within these networks, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as potential therapeutic targets because of their spatiotemporal expression patterns, context-dependent functions and ability to coordinate gene-expression programmes. Advances in RNA therapeutics provide tools to exploit these properties by targeting disease-associated transcripts and RNA-dependent interactions that are difficult to address with conventional small molecules or antibodies. Studies in NS tumour models have implicated lncRNAs as determinants of therapeutic responses, including DNA repair, apoptotic thresholds, stem-like states, mesenchymal-like plasticity, invasion, metabolic adaptation and stress responses, as well as intercellular communication within the tumour microenvironment. Targeting oncogenic lncRNAs may weaken resistance programmes and enhance the activity of partner treatments, providing a rationale for combinations that could maintain antitumour efficacy at lower drug doses. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for targeting lncRNAs to influence therapeutic response in NS tumours. The evidence is concentrated in gliomas, particularly glioblastoma, with additional studies in other entities. We summarise preclinical evidence for combining lncRNA-directed interventions with chemotherapy or radiotherapy, distinguishing changes in treatment sensitivity and resistance from quantitatively demonstrated synergy. We discuss targeting strategies, including antisense oligonucleotides, siRNAs and interaction-disrupting approaches, and consider translational challenges related to target selection, context-dependent biology, tumour heterogeneity, intracellular accessibility, delivery to tumours and potential toxicity to normal tissues. Collectively, these findings support lncRNAs as potentially actionable regulatory nodes and provide a foundation for developing more effective and better-tolerated combinatorial strategies in NS tumours.

articles.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine-Derived Natural Products: Potential Effects on Mitochondrial Energy Metabolism in Heart Failure.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Heart failure (HF), the end-stage of cardiovascular disease (CVD), affects over 64 million people globally. There is an alarming trend of earlier onset, which poses a substantial healthcare burden. Although guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) has significantly improved clinical outcomes, residual morbidity and mortality remain considerable, highlighting the need for additional therapeutic strategies. Mitochondrial energy metabolism (MEM) plays an important role in HF pathophysiology and represents a potential therapeutic target. Traditional Chinese Medicine-derived natural products (TCM-derived NPs) contain diverse bioactive constituents that may influence myocardial energy metabolism and related pathological processes, warranting further investigation into their potential role in HF management. PURPOSE: This review aims to synthesize current evidence on the involvement of MEM in HF and the potential regulatory effects of TCM-derived NPs. It further integrates mechanistic evidence with exploratory network pharmacology and molecular docking analyses to identify candidate compound-target relationships and discuss their translational implications. METHODS: The following keywords were used: "heart failure," "traditional Chinese medicine," "ATP synthesis," "oxidative phosphorylation," "fatty acid oxidation," "glucose metabolism," "mitochondrial membrane potential," "reactive oxygen species," "energy metabolism," "mitochondrial dynamics," "calcium signaling," and "energy coupling." Potential targets of NPs were obtained from the Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) Systems Pharmacology Database and Analysis Platform. We collected disease-related targets from Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man, GeneCards, and the Therapeutic Target Database. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis was performed using the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID). Protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed using STRING and analyzed in Cytoscape 3.10.0 to identify candidate hub genes. Ten representative bioactive compounds were separately examined through exploratory molecular docking with the candidate hub proteins. RESULTS: Herb-frequency analysis of 132 clinical studies identified 15 high-frequency Chinese medicinal herbs for subsequent computational analysis. The literature synthesis highlighted oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), fatty acid and glucose metabolism as key processes involved in myocardial energetic remodeling in HF. Separately, KEGG enrichment analysis identified pathways related to metabolic regulation, cellular stress, and inflammation, including lipid and atherosclerosis, PI3K-Akt, HIF-1, insulin, and TNF signaling pathways. PPI analysis prioritized AKT1, JUN, TP53, MAPK1, and MAPK3 in the MEM-related network and STAT3, TNF, TP53, IL6, and ESR1 in the inflammation-metabolism crosstalk network, yielding nine unique candidate hub genes after deduplication. Molecular docking of ten representative bioactive compounds with these nine candidate proteins yielded predicted docking scores ranging from -4.5 to -9.7kcal/mol. CONCLUSION: The available evidence supports MEM as an important component of HF pathophysiology and suggests that selected TCM-derived NPs may influence multiple MEM-related processes relevant to HF. By integrating mechanistic, clinical, and computational evidence, this review provides a structured framework for understanding NPs-MEM-HF relationships and offers a basis for future mechanistic validation and clinical translation.

articles.title: FAPI PET in Liver Fibrosis and Hepatobiliary Cancer: Linking Stromal Imaging to Radioligand Therapy.
articles.abstract: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) provides a shared imaging target in activated hepatic stroma and hepatobiliary tumor microenvironments. Whether this signal improves clinical decisions or identifies a therapeutic window remains unresolved. This review synthesizes imaging and translational evidence using a systematic search with a publication cutoff of 31 December 2025. Of 445 screened records, 64 reports are retained: 28 on hepatobiliary tumors, 6 on liver fibrosis, 23 on methodological, biodistribution or dosimetry questions, and 7 small series used for narrative illustration. These are report counts, not counts of independent cohorts. Small clinical studies suggest an association between hepatic uptake and fibrosis-related measures, while selected paired imaging studies report greater lesion conspicuity or detection with FAPI than with fluorodeoxyglucose PET. These findings do not establish superiority over standard liver MRI or elastography, transferable diagnostic thresholds, or improved patient outcomes. Inflammation, repair and background fibrosis limit specificity. For therapeutic translation, static uptake must be distinguished from ligand residence time, absorbed radiation dose and clinical benefit. Early radioligand-therapy reports describe feasibility alongside clinically important hematologic toxicity; safety and efficacy in cirrhotic liver populations remain unestablished. We therefore organize the evidence around tracer-specific pharmacokinetics, comparator choice and the joint assessment of lesion exposure and normal-organ vulnerability. Appraisal separates 302 entries using established tools from 104 descriptive reporting entries; non-independent checking and unresolved overlap limit certainty. The proposed clinical pathways are research frameworks requiring prospective validation, not recommendations for routine FAPI PET use.

articles.title: Operationalizing ICH E17 in Multiregional Clinical Trials: A Practical Roadmap for AI-Enabled and Quantitative Methods as Enabling Tools.
articles.abstract: ICH E17 harmonized the design and interpretation of multiregional clinical trials (MRCTs), yet almost a decade after adoption, its operationalization remains inconsistent across several areas: regional definition, assessment of regional heterogeneity, evaluation of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, pooling, bridging and extrapolation, and integration of real-world data. This White Paper offers a practical roadmap for operationalizing ICH E17 across the MRCT lifecycle (planning, conduct, and submission) in which artificial intelligence (AI), pharmacometric, and biostatistical methods are treated as enabling tools rather than as the primary subject. In this paper, for each decision point, we frame a context of use, decision consequence, validation expectation, bias assessment, documentation need, and likely regulatory engagement pathway, and we distinguish approaches that are usable today for operational support from those that may provide supportive evidence with appropriate validation and those that remain exploratory. We do not propose specific regulatory recommendations; rather, we intend this roadmap to stimulate cross-stakeholder discussion and the accumulation of shared, well-documented use cases that could, in time, inform future implementation-oriented guidance.

articles.title: The Pharmacological Basis of SGLT2 Inhibitor-Mediated Kidney Protection: From Proximal Tubular Mechanisms to Clinical Outcomes.
articles.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) worldwide despite advances in glycemic control, blood pressure management, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade. The introduction of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors has fundamentally changed the management of CKD by consistently reducing kidney disease progression and cardiovascular events in patients both with and without diabetes. These findings indicate that the benefits of SGLT2 inhibition extend beyond glucose lowering and reflect broader effects on cardiorenal physiology. This review examines the pharmacological mechanisms underlying SGLT2 inhibitor-mediated kidney protection, integrating experimental evidence with findings from major clinical outcome trials. Current evidence supports a hierarchical mechanistic model in which inhibition of proximal tubular sodium-glucose reabsorption represents the primary pharmacological event, restoring tubule-glomerular feedback, reducing intraglomerular pressure, and lowering tubular transport workload. These upstream hemodynamic and metabolic effects are thought to initiate downstream improvements in kidney oxygen balance, mitochondrial function, inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis, although the relative contribution of these pathways remains incompletely defined. We further examine how contemporary clinical trials validate this mechanistic framework across diverse CKD populations, including patients with and without diabetes and across a broad range of kidney function and albuminuria. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for phenotype-specific treatment strategies, rational combination therapy with complementary kidney-protective agents, and future directions in biomarker-guided precision medicine. Collectively, current evidence supports SGLT2 inhibitors as integrated cardiorenal therapies that modify fundamental determinants of CKD progression and provide the pharmacological foundation of contemporary kidney-protective treatment.

articles.title: Ceftazidime-avibactam monotherapy versus combination therapy for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infections: a secondary meta-analysis of predominantly critically ill cohorts.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial (CR-GNB) infections pose a critical threat to global public health, particularly in critically ill patients where treatment options are severely limited. Ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ/AVI) is a novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combination that has become a cornerstone therapy, yet its optimal use-as monotherapy or in combination with other agents-remains debated. OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the comparative efficacy, renal safety, and risk of on-treatment resistance emergence between CAZ/AVI monotherapy and combination therapy in adult patients with confirmed CR-GNB infections. Because individual-patient data were unavailable, pooled estimates are derived from mixed cohorts in which approximately 82% of participants were ICU-admitted critically ill patients (critically ill is defined as intensive care unit admission or APACHE II score ≥15). METHODS: This study is a secondary reanalysis of the aggregate dataset compiled by Hsu et al. (2024); no de novo systematic search was performed. Studies comparing CAZ/AVI monotherapy versus any combination regimen for the treatment of CR-GNB infections were eligible. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. The secondary outcomes included in-hospital, 14-day, and 90-day mortality; clinical cure; microbiological eradication; acute kidney injury (AKI); and on-treatment resistance emergence. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. The heterogeneity was assessed via I2 statistics, and publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test. Subgroup analyses were prespecified by pathogen type, infection site, combination regimen, geographic region, and study design. RESULTS: Twenty-five studies (23 retrospective cohorts and two prospective cohorts) enrolling 2,676 patients were included. The pooled 30-day mortality was 31.2% in the combination group and 32.8% in the monotherapy group, with no significant difference (RR = 0.91, 95% CI 0.79-1.04, P = 0.17; I2 = 34%). In-hospital mortality (RR = 1.00, 95% CI 0.78-1.27), 14-day mortality (RR = 1.54, 95% CI 0.26-9.28), and 90-day mortality (RR = 1.18, 95% CI 0.64-2.18) showed no significant between-group differences. Clinical cure rates were comparable (RR = 0.95, 95% CI 0.84-1.08; I2 = 39%). Microbiological eradication did not differ significantly between groups (RR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.00-1.33; P = 0.05; I2 = 31%). AKI incidence did not differ overall (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.69-1.22; I2 = 42%), although a post hoc analysis showed a non-statistically significant trend toward higher nephrotoxicity for polymyxin-containing combination regimens (RR = 1.28, 95% CI 0.94-1.74). On-treatment resistance emergence did not differ significantly between groups (RR = 0.71, 95% CI 0.42-1.21; P = 0.21; I2 = 19%). Subgroup analyses consistently showed no mortality benefit across pathogen types, infection sites, or specific combination agents. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings, and no significant publication bias was detected. CONCLUSION: This secondary meta-analysis, based on the aggregate dataset compiled by Hsu et al. (2024), suggests that CAZ/AVI combination therapy does not confer a statistically significant survival or clinical cure advantage over monotherapy in patients with CR-GNB infections, although it was associated with a non-significant trend toward higher microbiological eradication and lower on-treatment resistance emergence. Given the predominantly observational nature of the included studies, high-quality randomized controlled trials are urgently warranted to guide clinical decision-making. Until higher-certainty evidence becomes available, these very-low-certainty findings support cautious, individualized decision-making: CAZ/AVI monotherapy may be a reasonable default therapeutic option for many patients, whereas combination therapy could be considered in selected high-risk scenarios, carefully balancing the unproven microbiological signals against increased toxicity and cost.

articles.title: PEG length- and density-tuned stiffness of zoledronate-functionalized liposome for bone targeting by enhancing circulation.
articles.abstract: Bone cancers and skeletal metastases lead to severe bone destruction and high mortality. Current therapies including bisphosphonates, hormones, and RANKL inhibitors are hampered by non-specific biodistribution and dose-related toxicity. While zoledronate (ZOL)-modified PEGylated liposomes hold great promise for bone-targeted delivery, how PEG chain length and DSPE-PEG-ZOL doping density govern targeting performance remains incompletely understood. Herein, we constructed ZOL-functionalized PEGylated liposomes and systematically optimized these two key parameters. PEG10k was screened as the optimal chain length, and in vivo evaluation across 1%, 3% and 5% doping groups identified 3%ZOL-lip10k as the lead formulation with favorable biosafety, low immunogenicity, prolonged circulation and superior bone accumulation. Mechanistically, lower liposomal stiffness was associated with reduced protein adsorption and complement C3b deposition, prolonged circulation, and enhanced bone accumulation, supporting a relationship among liposomal mechanics, protein-corona formation, and in vivo targeting. DOX-loaded 3%ZOL-lip10k-DOX achieves high encapsulation efficiency, good stability and sustained release. It potently suppresses MDA-MB-231 proliferation and migration in vitro. In a breast cancer bone metastasis model, it retards tumor progression, alleviates cancer-induced osteolysis and preserves bone architecture with negligible systemic toxicity. This rationally optimized platform offers a robust strategy for precision bone-targeted therapy of skeletal metastases with promising clinical translation prospect.

articles.title: Liriopesides B ameliorates fine particulate matter-induced lung injury by directly targeting ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme E2 Q2 to dismantle the macrophage lactylation-neutrophil extracellular trap axis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure drives progressive lung injury characterized by aberrant neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). Current clinical management relies predominantly on broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory agents, which often carry severe risks of non-specific systemic immunosuppression and fail to resolve the underlying cell-cell pathological networks. Liriope platyphylla is a prominent traditional medicinal herb widely used in East Asia to treat respiratory conditions, yet its definitive active ingredients and direct molecular targets remain largely uncharacterized. METHODS: Utilizing an integrative framework spanning single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), surface plasmon resonance (SPR), molecular docking, and an in vivo macrophage-depleted adoptive transfer murine model, we investigated the therapeutic efficacy and specific molecular target of Liriopesides B (LPB), a natural steroidal saponin isolated from Liriope platyphylla. RESULTS: scRNA-seq and functional assays revealed that PM2.5 reprograms pulmonary macrophages into a hyper-glycolytic, lactylation-driven state, which paracrinally dictates downstream pathogenic neutrophil chemotaxis and NETosis. Mechanistically, the E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBE2Q2 acts as a critical immunometabolic checkpoint that regulates lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) to sustain this pro-inflammatory cascade. High-content imaging identified LPB as a potent inhibitor of this lactylation axis. Biophysical deconvolution confirmed that LPB directly binds to UBE2Q2 (KD =3.98 × 10-6 M), disrupting the macrophage-neutrophil crosstalk. Finally, cell-specific reconstitution assays validated that the in vivo protective benefits of LPB are strictly dependent on the macrophage-intrinsic UBE2Q2 axis. CONCLUSION: Our study decodes the UBE2Q2-LDHA-lactylation axis as a novel targetable vulnerability in environmental lung injury and highlights LPB as a mechanistically defined, natural product candidate for the targeted management of PM2.5-associated respiratory diseases.

articles.title: Feasibility of CYP2C19-guided clopidogrel therapy in community pharmacy: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Pharmacogenetic (PGx) testing holds promise for improving drug efficacy and safety by tailoring therapy to patients' genetic profiles. One of the most clinically relevant applications is CYP2C19 testing to guide clopidogrel therapy, particularly in cardiovascular patients. As accessible healthcare settings, community pharmacies may provide a practical model for delivering PGx services. This systematic review evaluates the feasibility of implementing CYP2C19 genetic testing for clopidogrel management in community pharmacy settings. METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, ProQuest, Cochrane Central, Scopus, and EBSCO was conducted from inception to 23 December 2025, following PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies assessed CYP2C19 testing in community pharmacies. Outcomes of interest included clinical, operational, economic, patient-reported, and provider-reported measures. RESULTS: Of 42 studies initially screened, three prospective studies met the inclusion criteria. All evaluated pharmacist-led CYP2C19 testing models in community pharmacies. Testing success rates were high (98%-100%). However, only the point-of-care testing enabled rapid turnaround times. Patient-reported perceptions were generally favorable, with most considering pharmacies appropriate for PGx testing. Pharmacists reported added clinical value but cited barriers such as reimbursement challenges, workflow integration, and knowledge gaps. Economic findings were mixed: point-of-care testing showed potential cost savings at higher rates of genotype-guided therapy modification, while reimbursement limitations hindered implementation in other settings. CONCLUSION: Community pharmacy-based PGx testing for clopidogrel provides preliminary evidence supporting operational feasibility. To support sustainable implementation, efforts should focus on establishing funding mechanisms, enhancing provider education, and integrating PGx testing into routine workflows.

articles.title: Structural characterisation of the effect of 5-chloroindole on orthosteric activation of murine 5-HT3A receptors.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: 5-HT3 receptors play a central role in gut-brain signalling, and their hyperactivity is associated with pathologies ranging from chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting to irritable bowel syndrome. While the principles governing 5-HT3R orthosteric pharmacology are well established (spanning antagonists, partial agonists and full agonists), structural insights into allosteric mechanisms remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the mechanisms by which a positive modulator of 5-HT3R, 5-chloroindole, potentiates agonist response by fine-tuning orthosteric activation of this receptor. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Here, we investigated the molecular basis of modulation by 5-chloroindole (5-CI), a selective positive allosteric modulator, using cryo-EM and electrophysiology. We present 5-HT3AR structures in the presence of 5-CI alone, as well as in combination with either submaximal concentrations of 5-HT or saturating concentrations of the partial agonist SMP-100. KEY RESULTS: Our results reveal that 5-CI potentiates 5-HT3R through a distinct mechanism involving co-occupancy of the orthosteric site and with additional modulation through an intersubunit site in the transmembrane domain. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: This mode of action is reminiscent of benzodiazepine modulation in GABAARs, yet it notably occurs within homomeric binding sites. Together, these findings establish the structural basis for the previously reported ago-allosteric mechanism of 5-CI, which becomes functionally apparent only in the presence of agonistic ligands.

articles.title: Glucocorticoid receptor dimerisation controls inflammation and tumour progression in colorectal cancer via a highly specific immune gene network.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The progression of ulcerative colitis (UC) to colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a major clinical challenge. Glucocorticoids (GCs) are widely used for the treatment of UC and also are included in therapeutic regimens for CRC. The transcriptional mechanisms through which GCs regulate inflammation and tumourigenesis via the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) remain incompletely understood. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: GRdim mice, expressing a dimerisation-defective GR with predominantly monomeric activity, were subjected to the azoxymethane/dextran sodium sulphate model of colitis-associated CRC. Inflammation, tumour development and survival were assessed and complemented by transcriptomic profiling, network analysis, tumour organoid experiments and cross-species comparisons. KEY RESULTS: Impaired GR dimerisation attenuated colon inflammation, as reflected by improved epithelial barrier integrity and reduced expression of pro-inflammatory genes. Tumourigenesis followed a biphasic pattern, with delayed tumour onset but accelerated tumour growth at later stages. Transcriptomic analyses revealed a distinct inflammatory signature in GRdim tumours, characterised by altered immune-related pathways and reduced gene expression linked to myeloid cell recruitment and activation. Integration with scRNA-seq datasets and tumour organoid studies indicated that altered GR activity affects both tumour cells and the tumour microenvironment. Cross-species analyses revealed an overlap between the gene signature distinguishing GRwt and GRdim murine tumours and gene expression patterns in human CRC that are associated with poor survival. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: GR dimerisation differentially contributes to the anti-inflammatory and tumour-related GC effects, thereby uncoupling the control of colitis from the regulation of tumour progression, highlighting potential limitations of selectively targeting GR monomer activity in therapeutic regimens.

articles.title: Short-term efficacy and safety of guselkumab for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis: a systematic review and meta-analysis with a pasi response-depth analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the short-term efficacy and safety of guselkumab in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and to explore whether its comparative advantage over adalimumab changes across increasingly stringent PASI response thresholds. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data were systematically searched from inception to April 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating guselkumab in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Two reviewers independently screened the literature, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.3. All efficacy and safety data were extracted at Week 16. In a post hoc exploratory response-depth analysis of the three head-to-head trials, the relative treatment effect of guselkumab versus adalimumab was examined across PASI75, PASI90, and PASI100 thresholds. RESULTS: Six RCTs comprising 997 patients in the guselkumab group, 625 in the adalimumab group, and 548 in the placebo group were included. At Week 16, guselkumab was associated with a significantly higher PASI90 response rate than adalimumab (RR = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.35-1.62, P < 0.001) and placebo (RR = 28.29, 95% CI: 16.69-47.96, P < 0.001). The exploratory head-to-head response-depth analysis showed a progressive increase in the relative advantage of guselkumab as the PASI target became more stringent: RR = 1.25 (95% CI: 1.18-1.32) for PASI75, 1.48 (1.35-1.62) for PASI90, and 1.85 (1.54-2.23) for PASI100. Corresponding crude response proportions across the three direct-comparison trials were 87.8% versus 71.0%, 70.8% versus 48.2%, and 35.3% versus 19.0%, respectively. Most short-term safety comparisons were imprecise and did not reach statistical significance. For upper respiratory tract infection versus adalimumab, the pooled estimate was RR = 1.69 (95% CI: 0.99-2.87; P = 0.05) based on two trials; the confidence interval only narrowly included the null and the comparison was underpowered. CONCLUSION: Beyond confirming greater Week 16 efficacy of guselkumab, this meta-analysis suggests that its relative advantage over adalimumab becomes more pronounced as the treatment target shifts from PASI75 toward near-complete or complete skin clearance. This response-depth pattern may be clinically relevant in an era in which PASI90 and PASI100 are increasingly used as treatment goals. Most evaluated short-term safety outcomes did not show statistically significant differences; however, estimates were imprecise and should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence.

articles.title: A pilot randomized feasibility trial of perioperative melatonin for cardiac arrhythmias during CPB weaning, sedative and analgesic medication use, and mechanical ventilation following CABG.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perioperative complications remain common following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Although melatonin may have cardioprotective and sedative-sparing effects, its feasibility and potential effects on early postoperative cardiac rhythm and recovery in patients undergoing CABG remain unclear. OBJECTIVES: To assess the feasibility of a future definitive randomized controlled trial (RCT) of perioperative melatonin in patients undergoing on-pump CABG and to obtain preliminary estimates of its effects on cardiac arrhythmias during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) weaning, duration of mechanical ventilation, and postoperative sedative and analgesic medication use. METHODS: In this pilot randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled feasibility trial, 22 adults undergoing elective on-pump CABG were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive oral melatonin (3 mg) or placebo nightly, from three nights before to three nights after surgery. Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, completeness of outcome assessment, and intervention safety. Exploratory clinical outcomes included cardiac arrhythmias during CPB weaning, duration of mechanical ventilation, and postoperative sedative and analgesic medication use. RESULTS: Twenty-two participants were randomized. The recruitment rate was 68.75%, while retention, protocol adherence, and completeness of outcome assessment were all 100%; no treatment-related adverse events were observed. Arrhythmias during CPB weaning occurred in 2 of 11 participants (18.2%) in each group (OR, 1.00; 95% CI: 0.11-8.73). The median duration of mechanical ventilation was 9.5 hours with melatonin and 15.0 hours with placebo (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the between-group location shift, -3.30 hours; 95% CI: -6.90 to 1.05). Postoperative sedative and analgesic medication use was generally comparable between groups, although the corresponding effect estimates were imprecise. CONCLUSION: Melatonin was feasible and well tolerated in this pilot cohort, with no treatment-related adverse events observed. The exploratory estimates were imprecise and do not provide evidence of efficacy, supporting a larger, adequately powered randomized trial to further evaluate the efficacy and safety of melatonin. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: IRCT20250206064666N1, date of registration: 2025-02-24.

articles.title: The next frontier of peptide therapeutics: from targeted conjugates (PDC/ODC) to AI-driven safety-by-design.
articles.abstract: The pharmaceutical landscape is witnessing a profound "Peptide Renaissance," driven primarily by the clinical success of GLP-1 receptor agonists and reinforced by engineering advanced drug delivery platforms. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of current trends in peptide-based drug development, using a target-localization framework that distinguishes molecular recognition from pharmacological action. We delineate the functional divergence between extracellular, cell-surface, and intracellular targeting, highlighting how peptides bridge the gap between small molecules and monoclonal antibodies. Central to this discussion is a comparative evaluation of next-generation conjugation technologies-Peptide-Drug Conjugates (PDCs) and Oligonucleotide-Drug Conjugates (ODCs)-against the backdrop of conventional Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs). Rather than a simple performance comparison, this analysis focuses on how the distinct structural architectures of these modalities dictate their pharmacological profiles. We examine the inherent trade-offs between the long systemic half-life of bulky, antibody-based scaffolds and the construct-dependent tissue distribution and immunogenicity of peptide and oligonucleotide delivery systems, thereby elucidating their respective strengths and limitations in targeting complex disease environments. PDCs can use peptide-mediated recognition or uptake to deliver therapeutic payloads, whereas ODCs deliver oligonucleotides that act intracellularly through mechanisms such as RNA interference or splice modulation. Furthermore, we explore the transformative role of generative Artificial Intelligence and structural algorithms, such as AlphaFold 3, in shifting the development paradigm toward a "Safety-by-Design" philosophy. By integrating predictive toxicology (e.g., pepADMET) into the nascent design phase, researchers may prioritize candidates for experimental testing. Importantly, the pharmacoeconomic case for this approach remains provisional rather than established. A retrospective analysis of AI-derived candidates reported Phase I success rates of approximately 80%-90% and a Phase II success rate of approximately 40%, comparable to historical Phase II averages. The limited sample and historical comparison do not establish a causal effect of AI or a peptide-specific economic benefit. We therefore present AI-guided safety-by-design as a proposed strategy for candidate prioritization, and set out explicitly the comparative evidence that would be required before claims of reduced development cost, shortened timelines, or improved affordability can be regarded as demonstrated.

articles.title: Single-cell multi-omics reveals cellular atlases and cell-cell interaction networks in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To summarize recent advances in single-cell multi-omics technologies in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), with a focus on cellular atlases, cellular heterogeneity, and intercellular communication networks in hepatic and extrahepatic tissues. METHODS: This narrative review synthesizes findings from studies identified primarily through PubMed searches supplemented by manual curation of reference lists. Search terms included "single-cell," "spatial transcriptomics," "MASLD," "NAFLD," "NASH," "MASH," "steatohepatitis," and "liver fibrosis." Studies applying single-cell transcriptomics, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, single-cell eQTL analysis, and integrative multi-omics approaches were included. The last literature search was conducted in July 2026. Results: Single-cell technologies have revealed key cellular alterations during MASLD progression, including disrupted hepatocyte metabolic zonation, heterogeneous activation states of hepatic stellate cells, macrophage functional reprogramming, immune cell dysfunction, and dynamic remodeling of the hepatic microenvironment. Spatial transcriptomics has further resolved the spatial organization of these cellular changes, whereas single-cell eQTL analyses have linked genetic susceptibility loci to cell-specific regulatory programs. Single-cell profiling of intestinal, adipose, and vascular tissues has expanded the understanding of extrahepatic contributions and gut-liver communication in MASLD. These advances provide a foundation for drug target identification, mechanistic understanding of current and investigational therapies, and assessment of treatment response at cellular resolution. CONCLUSION: Single-cell multi-omics is transforming MASLD research from tissue-level characterization toward cellular-resolution understanding, providing novel insights into disease stratification, therapeutic target discovery, and biomarker development, and advancing precision hepatology.

articles.title: Small Molecule-Protein Target Validation Strategies From Biophysical Binding Analysis to AI-Assisted Mechanistic Discovery.
articles.abstract: The rapid development of phenotypic screening, omics technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven drug discovery has accelerated the identification of bioactive small molecules and potential therapeutic targets. However, establishing reliable relationships between small molecules and their functional protein targets remains a major challenge in modern drug discovery. Precise characterization of small molecule-protein interactions is essential for elucidating mechanisms of action, optimizing lead compounds, improving target selectivity, and minimizing off-target effects. Nevertheless, phenotypic responses or individual binding assays alone are often insufficient to confirm bona fide pharmacological targets and define their functional consequences. This review summarizes current strategies for small molecule-protein target validation, including quantitative biophysical binding analysis, cellular target engagement assessment, stability- and affinity-based target identification, chemical proteomics, and structural characterization of ligand binding sites and key residues. We discuss how complementary approaches, such as surface plasmon resonance, biolayer interferometry, isothermal titration calorimetry, microscale thermophoresis, nuclear magnetic resonance, cellular thermal shift assay, and proteome-based technologies, provide distinct layers of evidence for defining molecular recognition, intracellular target engagement, and functional regulation. In addition, emerging applications of AI-assisted approaches in protein structure prediction, binding pocket identification, virtual screening, affinity prediction, and rational compound optimization are highlighted. We propose that reliable mechanism of action elucidation requires an integrated evidence framework combining computational prediction, biochemical validation, cellular evaluation, structural analysis, mutational studies, and functional confirmation. Such multidisciplinary strategies will strengthen target validation, reduce mechanistic uncertainty, facilitate rational drug optimization, and accelerate the development of safer and more effective therapeutics.

articles.title: Lung-to-heart delivery: Inhalable nanomedicine for cardiovascular disease treatment.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Although current pharmacological treatments have improved clinical outcomes, most primarily alleviate symptoms or modulate downstream pathways and have limited capacity to correct the underlying disease processes. Peptide- and nucleic acid-based therapeutics offer greater molecular specificity, but their clinical use is hampered by poor stability, low bioavailability, inefficient cardiac delivery, and off-target exposure after systemic administration. Pulmonary delivery provides a non-invasive alternative that bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism, enables rapid absorption, and may reduce systemic adverse effects. However, effective Lung-to-Heart delivery requires careful control of aerosolization, aerodynamic deposition, pulmonary retention, biological barrier transport, and myocardial accumulation. These considerations have stimulated growing interest in inhalable nanoparticle-based cardiovascular therapeutics, yet the relevant design principles and translational evidence remain scattered. In this review, we summarize the physicochemical properties, biomaterials, formulation methods, and inhaler technologies that govern the pulmonary deposition and biological fate of inhalable nanoparticles. We discuss their interactions with airway mucus, mucociliary clearance, pulmonary immune surveillance, and the alveolar-capillary barrier, as well as strategies for enhancing myocardial targeting. We further review emerging applications in heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and cardiomyopathy, with particular emphasis on the delivery of peptides, nucleic acids, and other precision therapeutics. Finally, we examine key challenges in pulmonary safety, pharmacokinetics, manufacturing reproducibility, scale-up, and regulatory evaluation. This review connects pulmonary drug delivery with cardiovascular nanomedicines and provides a practical basis for developing non-invasive, rapid-acting, and myocardium-targeted therapies.

articles.title: Beyond Dose Flexibility: How Much Precision Is Enough?
articles.abstract: Personalised medicines are frequently presented as a major application of pharmaceutical additive manufacturing because additive manufacturing enables the production of patient-specific dosage forms and highly flexible doses. However, increasingly fine dose resolution does not necessarily imply equivalent clinical benefit. Clinical and pharmacological variability may limit the accuracy with which patient-specific dose requirements can be determined, while the meaningful resolution of dose individualisation remains poorly established and is likely drug dependent. In this context, personalisation is proposed as a continuum of increasing flexibility rather than a binary distinction between conventional and additive manufacturing. This review examines the relationship between clinical, pharmacological, and manufacturing precision and considers whether increasingly precise dose individualisation is therapeutically meaningful. It further highlights how downstream variability may limit the clinical benefit obtainable from improvements in manufacturing precision. Finally, the role of additive manufacturing is considered beyond dose flexibility alone, and a conceptual framework is proposed for prioritising applications according to clinical need, distinct manufacturing advantages, and implementation feasibility.

articles.title: Pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib in advanced endometrial cancer: pharmacology, efficacy, safety and future perspectives.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib is an established post-platinum option for advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, particularly mismatch repair-proficient (pMMR) disease, in which single-agent programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade has limited activity. AREAS COVERED: This narrative review critically evaluates the pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, drug-interaction potential, efficacy and safety of pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib. Evidence from KEYNOTE-146, KEYNOTE-775, its 5-year analysis, ENGOT-en9/LEAP-001 and contemporary real-world cohorts was identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library from database inception to 14 August 2026, supplemented by ClinicalTrials.gov, regulatory documents and major congress proceedings. EXPERT OPINION: Pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib improves survival after platinum therapy in immune checkpoint inhibitor-naive advanced endometrial cancer, but substantial toxicity requires proactive monitoring and frequent lenvatinib dose modification. Its therapeutic position is being redefined by first-line chemoimmunotherapy and the negative ENGOT-en9/LEAP-001 trial, while post-immunotherapy efficacy, predictive biomarkers and prospectively validated dosing strategies remain key research priorities.

articles.title: Progesterone and diabetic wound repair: an evidence-gap review of indirect preclinical findings.
articles.abstract: The case for natural progesterone in diabetic wound repair rests on indirect preclinical findings, not demonstrated wound-healing efficacy. This evidence-gap review separates natural progesterone, its neuroactive metabolites and synthetic progestins, and distinguishes ligand interventions from studies of similarly named targets. Structured searches on 29 August 2026 and a targeted check on 30 September 2026 identified no natural-progesterone intervention measuring healing efficacy in a diabetic cutaneous wound. Diabetic-neuropathy experiments report selected neural improvements, but nerve conduction or intraepidermal fibre density does not establish functional re-epithelialisation, glycaemia-independent benefit or recovery of protective sensation at a wound. Findings in non-diabetic skin and other tissues are heterogeneous. Murine dorsal wounds also differ from human diabetic foot ulcers in contraction, loading, chronicity and vascular disease. A proposed neural mechanism must therefore be tested against epithelial and barrier outcomes, adequate perfusion and matched glycaemic exposure. Opposing metabolic and endothelial findings, together with compound- and route-specific safety concerns, preclude a general prediction of benefit. The review provides an auditable evidence map and falsifiable experimental priorities; it does not support clinical progesterone supplementation for diabetes-related foot ulcers.

articles.title: Anti-inflammatory potential of Astragalus polysaccharides: structural characteristics, mechanisms and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Astragalus polysaccharides (APS) are important bioactive macromolecules derived from Astragalus mongholicus Bunge, with potential anti-inflammatory properties. However, APS are structurally complex and highly heterogeneous natural polysaccharides and their structural characteristics, such as molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkage types, and branching patterns, may all affect their biological activities. In addition, factors such as plant source, medicinal part, extraction and processing methods, degradation, and structural modifications can further contribute to structural differences among various APS preparations. Due to the complexity of the fine structure of polysaccharides and the limitations of current methods for structural characterization and functional validation, the relationship between the specific structural features of APS and their anti-inflammatory activity has not yet been fully elucidated. In recent years, research into the anti-inflammatory mechanisms of APS has continued to deepen, encompassing multiple regulatory levels such as inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress, cellular homeostasis, macrophage function, and the gut microbiota. Based on this, this review focuses on the potential links between the structural characteristics of APS and their anti-inflammatory activity, and comprehensively summarizes the anti-inflammatory mechanisms of APS and research progress in inflammation-related diseases. At the same time, given the significant variations in experimental design and the depth of validation among existing structure-activity relationship studies, this review conducts a tiered evaluation of relevant structure-activity relationships and anti-inflammatory mechanisms based on specific APS preparations, taking into account the directness of evidence provided by different types of studies. By comparing the results of various studies, this review aims to further clarify the structural basis of the anti-inflammatory effect of APS and provide a reference for further research and development. Furthermore, this review discusses the pharmacokinetic characteristics of APS, novel delivery strategies, and the major challenges facing clinical translation.

articles.title: Systemic absorption and nephrotoxicity of antibiotic-loaded cement spacers: pharmacokinetic principles and clinical risk management.
articles.abstract: Antibiotic-loaded polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) spacers are widely used during staged revision for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) to provide high local antimicrobial exposure, but they are not pharmacologically isolated from the systemic circulation. Human pharmacokinetic studies demonstrate measurable vancomycin and aminoglycoside concentrations after implantation, sometimes persisting for weeks, while clinical studies report heterogeneous rates of acute kidney injury (AKI) across populations and spacer regimens. Risk cannot be inferred from grams of antibiotic per 40 g of cement alone: formulation concentration, total implanted drug mass, cement mass, release kinetics, spacer geometry, concurrent systemic therapy, perioperative hemodynamics, and patient-specific renal clearance are related but distinct determinants of systemic exposure. This Mini Review integrates PMMA elution principles with quantitative human evidence, separates evidence of spacer-derived absorption from associations with AKI and from general perioperative risk factors, and proposes a pragmatic risk-management framework. The framework is not prospectively validated. Safer use requires stable-baseline renal risk assessment, explicit documentation of total antibiotic and cement doses, coordinated local and systemic prescribing, early monitoring in high-risk inpatients, selective serum drug measurement when exposure or toxicity is suspected, and multidisciplinary escalation for persistent toxicity. Future studies should use standardized dose, sampling, exposure, and KDIGO-defined renal outcome metrics and should distinguish spacer-derived from intravenously administered drug exposure.

articles.title: Informing the development of β-lactam-β-lactamase inhibitor combinations through a comparison of in vitro data.
articles.abstract: Mortality rates associated with antimicrobial resistance are increasing at an alarming rate and are becoming one of the most serious threats to global health. Paradoxically, investment in the development of new antibacterial agents is limited as a result of multiple factors, including resistance, which have the potential to shorten the clinical lifespan of an antibacterial agent. Improvements in the tools used to predict the success or failure of drug candidates have been shown to reduce the overall cost of the drug discovery process. β-Lactamases are drug-modifying enzymes that can hydrolyse and inactivate the β-lactam antibiotics. The development of β-lactamase inhibitors (BLIs) can enable the re-sensitisation of bacteria previously resistant to the β-lactams (BLs). There are nine β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) combinations available for use in clinical practice. This review presents a summary of the in vitro performance of the nine currently marketed BL/BLI combinations in synergy assays, serving as a comparative reference for researchers developing new combinations.

articles.title: Wnt/β-catenin-mTOR crosstalk in TSC-associated epilepsy: pharmacological evidence and therapeutic opportunities.
articles.abstract: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), caused by pathogenic variants in TSC1 or TSC2, is frequently associated with early-onset and drug-resistant epilepsy. Loss of hamartin-tuberin activity causes Rheb-dependent mTORC1 hyperactivation and provides the mechanistic basis for mTOR-directed treatment with everolimus, but mTORC1 activation alone does not fully account for variation in seizure burden or treatment response. Evidence from biochemical and disease-model studies indicates that TSC1/TSC2 also interacts with canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling through GSK3β and Axin, while cellular metabolism may provide an additional point of convergence through AMPK-dependent regulation of TSC2. This narrative review examines the biochemical, neuronal, human-tissue, pharmacological, and clinical evidence for this Wnt-GSK3β-TSC2-mTOR framework and distinguishes established findings from context-limited, emerging, and hypothetical relationships. Everolimus remains the established mechanism-based therapy for TSC-associated refractory seizures, whereas metformin has the strongest TSC-specific clinical signal among the investigational metabolic approaches discussed. GLP-1 receptor agonists and direct GSK3β modulation remain preclinical or mechanistically speculative in this setting. Gene- and RNA-based approaches provide emerging precedents for pathway-selective intervention, but none has directly targeted the Wnt-GSK3β-TSC2 interface. The principal unresolved question is whether this signaling relationship operates in human TSC epileptogenic tissue. Direct tissue-level validation, followed by selective pathway interrogation and adequately powered therapeutic studies, is needed before Wnt-directed strategies can be considered clinically relevant in TSC-associated epilepsy.

articles.title: Blood-brain barrier-penetrant pharmacological strategies for neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease: small molecules and engineered peptides.
articles.abstract: Recognition of Alzheimer's disease (AD) as a neuroinflammatory disorder, alongside amyloid-β and tau pathology, necessitates the development of innovative therapies capable of overcoming blood-brain barrier (BBB)-mediated limitations to brain drug delivery. This review discusses current efforts to develop BBB-permeable small molecules and peptide-based therapies targeting the neuroimmune modulators TREM2, the NLRP3 inflammasome, RIPK1, and the cGAS-STING signaling pathway, with consideration of the concept of the neurovascular paradox. Despite promising recent developments, the trade-off between permeability, selectivity, and cytotoxicity remains a significant issue. The current findings indicate that BBB penetration, the timing of microglial targeting, immunosuppressive effects, and neuroimmune homeostasis should be considered when seeking to modulate neuroinflammation effectively. Novel delivery systems, such as those using cell-penetrating peptide shuttles and antibody-based transport systems, may help address BBB limitations, and biomarker-guided treatment is increasingly important. Overall, this review reframes brain drug delivery not only as a function of pharmacokinetic parameters but also as part of a system integrating neurovascular physiology, neuroimmunology, and medicinal chemistry.

articles.title: Immune idiosyncratic DILI by ICIs: specifics of published cases based on evidence as evaluated for causality by RUCAM.
articles.abstract: The diagnosis of immune idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (iDILI) by immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is blurred by the heterogeneity of causality attribution in cancer patients; this requires information gaps to be filled through the collection of cases evaluated for causality by the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM). RUCAM was used in 8/11 reports (73%), providing a rather homogeneous study cohort for the following manifestation specifics: (1) consensus among the eight RUCAM-based reports that iDILI by ICIs has an immune basis; (2) age of most patients > 60 years; (3) male gender dominated by a factor ranging from 1.5- to 4.0-fold; (4) clinical manifestations at admission included weakness, vomiting, epigastric pain, and itching but not necessarily jaundice; (5) serum activities of ALT up to 3,111 U/L, with ALP up to 2,459 U/L and total bilirubin up to 300 μmol/L; (6) RUCAM-based ratio (R) revealing a pattern of hepatocellular liver injury (42%), cholestatic (39%), and mixed liver injury (19%); (7) therapeutic options require a case-by-case decision, as the natural course is variable among the cancer patients; (8) although treatment with steroids and/or ursodeoxycholic acid was commonly effective, a therapy decision has to consider whether the use of the implicated ICI should be stopped or continued; (9) prognosis depends largely on disease severity; (10) among the cancer patients with DILI by ICIs, 22% died during follow-up, mostly after progress of underlying disease. In brief, RUCAM use allows for the correct description of clinical manifestations, but more diagnostic efforts are needed for iDILI by ICIs if associated with the novel autoimmune pancreatitis type AIP-3, reflecting pancreatic involvement with possible secondary sclerosing cholangitis.

articles.title: Endocrine and enzymatic control of teleost osmoregulation: insights into physiological adaptations.
articles.abstract: Teleost fishes inhabit environments that differ markedly in salinity and ionic composition and therefore require highly coordinated mechanisms to maintain water, electrolyte, and acid-base homeostasis. Osmoregulation integrates the functions of the gills, gastrointestinal tract, kidney, and endocrine system, with ion-transporting enzymes and membrane proteins serving as major molecular effectors. This review synthesizes current knowledge of endocrine and enzymatic regulation of teleost osmoregulation, with particular emphasis on the renal mechanisms that provide a framework for renal pharmacology and translational research. In freshwater, teleosts actively acquire ions and eliminate excess water through the production of dilute urine, whereas seawater teleosts drink seawater, absorb water and ions through the gastrointestinal tract, and actively excrete excess ions through the gills while producing relatively small volumes of urine. Hormones including prolactin, cortisol, growth hormone, thyroid hormones, and stanniocalcin coordinate these responses through effects on ionocytes, renal transport processes, and epithelial permeability. Na+/K+-ATPase and other ion-transport systems provide the energetic and electrochemical basis for osmoregulation, whereas aquaporins (AQPs) contribute to regulated renal water transport. Importantly, teleost kidneys exhibit a remarkable capacity for repair and de novo nephron formation following injury, providing a valuable experimental model for investigating nephrotoxicity and renal regeneration. Pharmacological studies using established nephrotoxicants such as gentamicin and cisplatin demonstrate the utility of zebrafish for evaluating drug-induced renal injury. However, direct pharmacological manipulation of specific renal AQPs remains comparatively underdeveloped, and species-specific differences limit direct extrapolation to humans. We therefore distinguish conserved mechanisms from species-specific observations and identify opportunities for integrating renal transport physiology, toxicology, pharmacology, and regenerative biology. Collectively, teleost models provide an important platform for understanding aquatic adaptation and for generating mechanistic hypotheses relevant to mammalian renal pharmacology.

articles.title: Model-informed AUC-guided monitoring of enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium: population pharmacokinetics and clinical transferability.
articles.abstract: Delayed, variable absorption and enterohepatic recirculation complicate estimation of mycophenolic acid (MPA) exposure after enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium (EC-MPS) administration. This narrative review examines nine population pharmacokinetic development studies and related limited-sampling and clinical evidence to assess procedures for estimating total plasma MPA area under the concentration-time curve over 12 h (AUC0-12h). Selected three- or four-sample regression and Bayesian procedures support AUC estimation, mainly in adult kidney transplant recipients. Validation against densely sampled noncompartmental AUC assesses agreement with a sampling-based reference; comparison with full-profile AUC from the same model assesses recovery of model-derived exposure from fewer samples. Patient holdout alone does not ensure independent validation of sampling schedules, and sparse low-exposure data limit assessment of underexposure detection. The commonly used 30-60 mg h/L target is supported mainly by mycophenolate mofetil studies in kidney transplantation and requires assay- and indication-specific interpretation. Direct EC-MPS studies support exposure-outcome associations and the feasibility of concentration-guided dosing, while evidence of improved clinical outcomes remains limited. These findings guide selection of candidate monitoring procedures by matching the estimator, sampling schedule, assay and exposure target to the intended population and dosing decision.

articles.title: Catheter tip placement for intrathecal therapy in refractory cancer pain: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intrathecal drug delivery (IDD) provides continuous administration of analgesics into the intrathecal space. Although catheter tip placement is considered important for treatment success, evidence of its impact on long-term clinical outcomes remains limited, particularly when considering pain distribution, cancer type, and the intrathecal medication used. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the evidence of catheter tip positioning in patients with refractory cancer pain. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EMBASE were systematically searched from inception to October 2025. Studies including patients with refractory cancer pain treated with implanted IDD were included. Study quality was assessed using a modified Downs and Black checklist. Meta-regression was performed to evaluate associations between treatment success and catheter tip location, pain distribution, and intrathecal medication type. RESULTS: Of 8,414 identified articles, 23 studies were included (14 in meta-analysis). Catheter tip placement descriptively corresponded to cancer type and pain location. However, meta-regression analyses showed no significant association between treatment success and catheter tip location (p = 0.914), pain location (p = 0.407), or intrathecal medication category (p = 0.937). CONCLUSIONS: Descriptive findings support anatomically guided catheter placement, but the available evidence is insufficient to determine whether catheter tip location or other examined factors are associated with treatment success. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251150374 identifier is CRD420251150374.

articles.title: Teacher training for the school-based prevention of alcohol and other drug use: a scoping review with implications for pharmaceutical sciences.
articles.abstract: Teacher training is integral to school-based prevention of alcohol and other psychoactive substance use, yet its content, implementation, and evaluation are reported unevenly. To map school-based prevention initiatives incorporating teacher training and examine their structure, evaluation, and documented pharmacological and toxicological content. This scoping review followed JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR. PubMed/MEDLINE, ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and LILACS/BVS were searched without formal publication-date or language restrictions. Multiple reports on the same initiative were linked for initiative-level synthesis. The review included 198 reports representing 142 initiatives, of which 138 underwent cross-cutting coding. Teacher training differed in delivery, duration, implementation support, and evaluation. Among the 138 initiatives, 108 (78.3%) documented some form of program evaluation, but only 13 (9.4%) reported independent or external evaluation. Teacher-training outcomes were reported in 72 initiatives (52.2%), and student outcomes in 73 (52.9%); these indicators did not establish effectiveness attributable to training. Specific toxicological content was documented in 22 initiatives (15.9%), broad or nonspecific mentions in 30 (21.7%), and insufficient information to determine its presence in 86 (62.3%). Risk communication was documented in 62 initiatives (44.9%). Teacher training was embedded in heterogeneous school-based prevention programs, with uneven implementation support and evaluation. Limited reporting of scientific content does not demonstrate its absence from training. Clearer descriptions of curricula and implementation conditions, together with evaluations distinguishing teacher learning, classroom practice, and student outcomes, are needed. Collaboration between Pharmaceutical Sciences and education may support evidence-informed, age-appropriate, and non-stigmatizing prevention content.

articles.title: Inhaled cannabis and oral alcohol: driving performance and subjective driving confidence in a human laboratory study.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Cannabis is the most commonly detected drug (second only to alcohol) among crash-involved drivers. Determining cannabis effects on driving performance is imperative to public health. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to assess a range of inhaled cannabis doses and an intoxicating dose of oral alcohol on simulated driving outcomes and subjective driving confidence. METHODS: Healthy participants who used cannabis (n = 9) were enrolled in this within-subject, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled, outpatient human laboratory study. Participants completed five experimental sessions to examine the effects of inhaled cannabis (0, 15, 30 mg THC; 15 mg THC + 7.5 mg CBD) and oral alcohol (0, 0.8 g/kg [15% less for women]). Data were collected at baseline and for 7.5 h after drug administration. RESULTS: Alcohol produced robust impairment on simulated driving performance outcomes (e.g., decreased lateral control; p<0.05). Cannabis decreased brake force and altered headway distance during obstacle navigation (p<0.05). All active doses of cannabis and alcohol decreased driving confidence (e.g., willingness to operate a real vehicle; p<0.05) and increased ratings of abuse potential (e.g., drug liking, p<0.05). High dose cannabis (30 mg) and alcohol increased subjective ratings of impairment and sedation (p<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Cannabis did not produce profound alcohol-like driving impairment; however, it was not without risk, and driving impairment was evident. All active cannabis doses decreased participants' driving confidence, while the highest dose of cannabis (30 mg) and alcohol increased self-reported impairment and sedation. Overall, even in a sample of near-daily cannabis users, cannabis negatively impacted driving performance, decreased driving acuity, and reduced confidence in safe driving ability.

articles.title: Long-acting targeted delivery of TNF-α-derived peptide for enhanced anti-renal fibrosis treatment via activation of the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway.
articles.abstract: Renal fibrosis is an excessive accumulation of the extracellular matrix in the kidney in response to injury, and thus leading to renal function loss, which lacks effective therapeutic agents in clinical settings. Herein, we engineered a multifunctional protein Z-IgBD-P16 derived from IgG-binding domain (IgBD) to extend the serum half-life and platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ)-specific affibody ZPDGFRβ to enhance fibrotic kidney-targeted distribution of P16, an apoptosis-inducing TNF-α-derived peptide that specific binding to TNF-α receptor 1 (TNFR1) but not receptor 2 (TNFR2), as a model drug for renal fibrosis treatment. Z-IgBD-P16 possesses excellent targeting ability to myofibroblasts in TGF-β1-activated NIH3T3 cells and fibrotic kidneys in UUO mice. Z-IgBD-P16 also extends the serum half-life in the fibrotic kidney in the UUO mice model of renal fibrosis. Coupled with its high targeting specificity, the extended serum half-life of Z-IgBD-P16 confers sustained long-acting potential. Z-IgBD-P16 significantly mitigates renal fibrosis in in vitro cell and in vivo mice model of renal fibrosis by specific inducing myofibroblast apoptosis via the mitochondrial-dependent pathway. These findings suggest that Z-IgBD-P16 proves effective in treating renal fibrosis and warrants further investigation for its therapeutic potential.

articles.title: Market analysis of chondroitin and glucosamine as dietary supplements.
articles.abstract: Chondroitin and glucosamine are widely used as dietary supplements for osteoarthritis (OA), despite inconsistent clinical evidence and limited regulatory oversight. Concerns remain regarding efficacy, bioavailability, safety and discrepancies between marketed claims and scientific data. To investigate the characteristics of marketed chondroitin and glucosamine dietary supplements and to evaluate the clinical evidence regarding their efficacy and safety in OA. This study combined a cross-sectional market analysis of 110 dietary supplements with a structured review of clinical studies. Supplements were analyzed with respect to composition, dosage, pricing, labelling and marketing strategies. A PubMed search was conducted to identify clinical trials and meta-analyses investigating orally administered chondroitin and/or glucosamine in OA patients. Eligible studies were analyzed descriptively due to heterogeneity. The product analysis revealed highly variable pricing, with substantial cost differences and no clear link between price and clinical effectiveness. Marketing strategies often relied on packaging and presentation to imply scientific validation, frequently without sufficient supporting evidence. The available clinical evidence does not provide a consistent or robust basis for confirming the efficacy of chondroitin and glucosamine in OA. The effectiveness of chondroitin and glucosamine in OA in treating OA is questionable, a major problem being the poor bioavailability. Overall, the field is plagued by poor scientific evidence.

articles.title: From regulatory approval to patient access: A comparative analysis of biosimilar market entry timelines in Japan, the USA, and the EU.
articles.abstract: Biosimilar approval lag and biosimilar loss, the latter also referred to as the biosimilar void, remain important challenges particularly in Japan compared with the United States of America (USA) and the European Union (EU). However, regulatory approval does not necessarily translate into timely patient access. Although biosimilar approval lag has been widely discussed, international comparisons of patient access after regulatory approval remain limited. We evaluated biosimilar approval lag, market entry lag, and patient access time (defined as the interval between regulatory approval and first commercial launch). Commercial launch was used as the earliest measurable milestone of patient access, rather than as a measure of subsequent biosimilar uptake in clinical practice. Analyses were conducted using publicly available data from the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA), the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the European Medicines Agency (EMA), supplemented by company press releases. The median patient access time was shortest in Japan (6 months) compared with the USA (15 months) and the EU (17 months). Despite a persistent approval lag, patient access to biosimilars in Japan was frequently comparable to, or earlier than, that in the USA and the EU, largely because of shorter approval-to-launch intervals. Regulatory approval timing alone is insufficient to assess patient access to biosimilars. Ensuring timely patient access requires a comprehensive approach that integrates post-approval pathways, including market entry, pricing, and reimbursement, with coordinated efforts across the full biosimilar lifecycle.

articles.title: Morusin induces GSDME-dependent pyroptosis in non-small cell lung cancer via the angiotensin II receptor type 2.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, its 5-year survival rate continues to be unsatisfactory. Current therapies are often limited by resistance, toxicity, or poor efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for novel strategies. METHOD: We performed a high-throughput compound screen for inducing cell death in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Combined with lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assays, cell death morphology observation, and propidium iodide (PI) staining, we confirmed the cell death mode as pyroptosis. Then, we conducted a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen to identify the critical regulator of compound-induced pyroptosis. RESULTS: The screening results showed that morusin is a trigger of gasdermin E (GSDME)-mediated pyroptosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Importantly, morusin suppresses tumor growth in vivo. Through a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen, we further demonstrated that angiotensin II receptor type 2 (AGTR2) as a critical regulator of morusin-induced pyroptosis, acting via activation of the caspase-3-GSDME signaling cascade. Notably, morusin also upregulated AGTR2 expression in NSCLC cells. In an NSCLC mouse model, morusin treatment potently suppressed wild-type tumor growth, whereas its antitumor efficacy was substantially diminished in AGTR2-knockout tumors. CONCLUSION: Our study reveals a novel mechanism underlying the antitumor effect of morusin, establishes AGTR2 as a potential therapeutic target, and provides a rationale for pyroptosis-based therapy for NSCLC.

articles.title: Elsholtzia Bodinieri vaniot dichloromethane extract exerts anti-inflammatory effects in acute lung injury mice by regulating the CCR1 and FLT1.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute lung injury (ALI) is a disease characterized by diffuse dysfunction leading to systemic inflammation, increased vascular permeability and loss of alveolar epithelial cell function. Elsholtzia bodinieri Vaniot is a traditional folk medicinal and edible plant endowed with heat-clearing(Qingre) and detoxifying efficacies. METHODS: The dichloromethane fraction of E. bodinieri Vaniot extract (EBED) was isolated and evaluated for anti-inflammatory activity. Chemical profiling of EBED was performed using untargeted metabolomics. Putative target genes of EBED were predicted through bioinformatics analysis, and the anti-inflammatory effects of EBED were assessed both in vitro and in vivo using a model of acute lung injury (ALI). Mechanistic validation focused on CC chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1)- and Fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (FLT1)-mediated downstream signaling pathways by Western blot and inflammatory mediator detection. In addition, the impact of EBED on gut microbiota composition was evaluated in ALI mice via fecal microbiome analysis, with particular attention to changes in the relative abundances of specific bacterial genera. RESULTS: EBED exerted markedly superior anti-inflammatory activity compared with other fractions. A total of 1775 chemical metabolites were identified in EBED. Bioinformatics analysis predicted that CCR1 and FLT1 serve as potential target genes for EBED to exert anti-inflammatory activity against ALI, which was subsequently validated in inflammatory pathways. In vitro and in vivo experiments collectively demonstrated that EBED mitigates inflammatory responses via modulating CCR1 and FLT1, as well as their downstream signaling cascades including CCR1/Ca2+, FLT1/PRKCA and FLT1/PRKD2, thereby regulating the expression of inflammatory mediators. Furthermore, EBED remodeled the gut microbiota structure in ALI mice. Specifically, the abundances of beneficial bacteria including Akkermansia, Lactobacillus, Ruminococcus and Coriobacteriaceae_UCG-002 were markedly elevated, while those of harmful bacteria such as Rikenellaceae, Tyzzerella and Paraprevotella were distinctly decreased. CONCLUSION: In summary, the EBED demonstrates potent anti-inflammatory activity against ALI. This effect is mediated through the modulation of key target genes CCR1 and FLT1. Additionally, EBED exerts a favorable remodelling effect on the gut microbiota of ALI mice. These findings position EBED as a promising functional food ingredient and a potential therapeutic candidate for the prevention and treatment of ALI.

articles.title: Cost-effectiveness of datopotamab deruxtecan versus chemotherapy as a first-line treatment for patients with advanced triple-negative breast cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The phase III TROPION-Breast02 trial demonstrated improved progression-free and overall survival with datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd) versus chemotherapy in patients with previously untreated advanced triple-negative breast cancer who were ineligible for immunotherapy. This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of Dato-DXd from the perspectives of the United States (U.S.) and Chinese healthcare systems. METHODS: A three-state partitioned survival model was developed using TROPION-Breast02 data, with a 10-year horizon and 21-day cycles. Costs and utilities were obtained from public databases and published literature. The primary outcome was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER), expressed as cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) gained. Willingness-to-pay thresholds were $150,000/QALY in the U.S. and $27,906/QALY in China. Sensitivity and scenario analyses assessed uncertainty and the robustness of the findings, and exploratory subgroup analyses were performed. RESULTS: Compared with chemotherapy, Dato-DXd increased costs by $565,572.29 and QALYs by 0.44 in the U.S., yielding an ICER of $1,287,001.65/QALY. In China, the corresponding increases were $39,052.50 and 0.42 QALYs, yielding an ICER of $92,640.82/QALY. Price reductions of approximately 62.43% in the U.S. and 28.83% in China were required to reach the respective cost-effectiveness thresholds. Progression-free survival utility and Dato-DXd price were the most influential parameters in one-way sensitivity analyses. In exploratory scenario analyses, limiting treatment duration to the reported median yielded cost-effective results in both countries. Assuming unchanged efficacy, a hypothetical reduction in the Dato-DXd dose from 6 to 4 mg/kg made it cost-effective in China but not in the U.S. Exploratory subgroup analyses yielded conclusions consistent with the base-case findings. CONCLUSION: At the modeled prices and under the base-case assumptions, Dato-DXd was not cost-effective compared with chemotherapy in either country. Price reductions could improve its cost-effectiveness. Results were sensitive to assumptions about treatment duration. The potential economic benefits of reduced-dose or fixed-duration strategies depend on clinical confirmation of maintained efficacy and acceptable safety.

articles.title: Protective effects of AKBA against hypoxia-induced cognitive dysfunction: potential involvement of SLC2A1, PTGS1, and BCL2L1.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hypoxia-induced cognitive impairment (HICI) is associated with neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and gut microbiota dysbiosis, highlighting the need for effective neuroprotective interventions. Acetyl-11-keto-β-boswellic acid (AKBA), a bioactive triterpenoid derived from frankincense, possesses anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, but its protective effects against hypoxia-associated cognitive dysfunction remain insufficiently understood. METHODS: This study investigated the neuroprotective potential of AKBA administered concurrently with hypoxic exposure and explored its associated molecular alterations. Network pharmacology, transcriptomic analysis, molecular similarity assessment, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations were integrated to identify and prioritize candidate proteins. The protective effects of AKBA were subsequently evaluated in mice exposed to normobaric hypoxia (12.7% O2) for 10 days. RESULTS: AKBA administration attenuated hypoxia-associated cognitive deficits, accompanied by reduced inflammatory and oxidative stress markers, increased BDNF levels, decreased TUNEL-positive staining, and preservation of MBP immunoreactivity.
